events.credibility_reason: Whether any proof was published is disputed (Wikipedia vs Chase 2020); the 1878 source was not opened.
Withdrawn by the author in v2 (19 July 2016) for flaws in the statistical method.
The page's 1.5x10^15 headline conflicts with its description of the run as interrupted, and it carries unreconciled captions (969 at 1.6931x10^15; G(Pi(6.150x10^15))=800).
The author labels central parts informal, conditional or partial ('None of this is proved yet'), and no engagement was found.

why: The statement is about the infinite prime sequence at every depth. Every computational check (Kilgrove–Ralston, Odlyzko, Plouffe, Colonna, Shimizu) only verifies finitely many initial segments, so I scored them instances (F5). Chase 2020, Chase–Hunter–Tao 2026 (Cramér random model), Granville (sieved sequences), Muney (finite Gilbreath sequences), Ross (continuous-model constants) and Eppstein (non-prime sequences) all settle changed questions, so I scored them variant. The Chase–Hunter–Tao inverse theorem is conditional on an unproved Cramér-type gap bound and leaves its obstructions open. That makes it a reduction, not a case, and its random-model theorem is the paper's main result. The authors themselves say the conjecture remains open. AI: Chase–Hunter–Tao used Gemini only for figure code, and Pith is an AI referee, so both count as none. Muney's disclosure names no system and the paper is a variant anyway. Shimizu's bare line 'AI-assisted (Claude, Anthropic; OpenAI Codex).' says nothing about any mathematics in a package that reproduces a 1993 computation, so it is none (F12); that event is discarded as instances in any case.
doubts: Shimizu's AI disclosure is generic. If Claude or Codex wrote the verification code, that is still not mathematics in the result. Muney's 'conjecture generation' disclosure may have contributed to theorems, but those theorems concern finite sequences, not the primes.
